one_liner: Single-header SDSL-compatible byte-alphabet wavelet tree (wt_fbb) using fixed-block compression boosting, aimed at faster, smaller FM-indexes than SDSL's.
what_it_does: Provides one class, wt_fbb, in include/wt_fbb.hpp: a wavelet tree over a byte sequence that is meant to be plugged into an SDSL FM-index (the combination is the 'Faster Minuter' index of Gog, Karkkainen, Kempa, Petri and Puglisi, DCC 2016 and Algorithmica 2019). It is built from a raw uint8_t buffer or an sdsl::int_vector_buffer<8> and answers access (operator[]), rank(i, c) and inverse_select(i), with SDSL-style serialize/load/swap. It has no select() member and no lex_count or interval_symbols, so it is a partial replacement for SDSL wavelet trees, not a full one.
how_it_is_fast: Fixed-block compression boosting: the text is cut into superblocks (2^20 symbols by default) and variable-size blocks, and each block gets its own small Huffman-shaped wavelet tree over only the symbols that occur in it, so the per-block alphabet and tree height stay small and a rank query touches a few cache lines. Precomputed rank counts at hyperblock (2^32), superblock and block boundaries, plus a navigational block header (ADD_NAVIGATIONAL_BLOCK_HEADER), let a query skip tree navigation for boundary ranks. The bitvectors are sdsl::hyb_vector (hybrid bitvectors) by default, and any SDSL bitvector with a rank_1_type can be substituted for speed.
when_to_use: Building a byte-alphabet FM-index (DNA, text, BWT of a log or corpus) on SDSL where count/locate speed or index size matters and you can test against SDSL's own wt_huff or wt_hutu choices.
Highly compressible or locally skewed BWTs, where per-block Huffman shaping gives compression boosting without the cost of optimal partitioning.
Research or benchmarking of FM-index variants that needs the reference implementation of the Algorithmica 2019 fixed-block-boosting wavelet tree.
Workloads dominated by rank and LF-mapping (backward search, inverse_select), which is what the class implements.
when_not_to_use: You need select on the sequence, lex_count or interval_symbols (bidirectional or range searches): wt_fbb does not implement them.
Alphabets larger than 256 symbols or integer sequences: the class is byte-alphabet only (sdsl::byte_alphabet_tag, uint8_t symbols).
You need a maintained library: 2 commits, version 0.1.0, last commit 2021-05-18, no tests, no build files and no benchmark code in the repo.
You need numbers you can check before adopting it: the repo has no measurements, and the paper's tables could not be read here, so the speed and space win over SDSL is unverified.
Your project does not already use sdsl-lite: the header depends on SDSL types throughout.

integration.min_toolchain: not documented; uses C++11 features (defaulted constructors, move semantics) and GCC packed attributes; 'tested on Linux/PC'
integration.platforms: Linux on x86-64 per README ('tested on Linux/PC'); relies on __attribute__((packed)) and 32-bit pointer casts into byte arrays, so other compilers or strict-alignment targets are untested
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the query methods are const and the class has no mutable members, so concurrent read-only queries look safe, but this is not promised
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — follows SDSL's wavelet tree concept (wt_tag, byte alphabet, operator[], rank, inverse_select, serialize/load) so it can be a csa_wt template argument for backward search, but lacks select, lex_count and interval_symbols that some SDSL algorithms call

gotchas: Configuration is by #define macros at the top of the header (ADD_NAVIGATIONAL_BLOCK_HEADER, SPARSE_SUPERBLOCK_MAPPING, ALLOW_VARIABLE_BLOCK_SIZE, FAST_CONSTRUCTION), so they apply to every instantiation in the translation unit.

The off-by-default SPARSE_SUPERBLOCK_MAPPING path's load() calls sdsl::load without the stream argument and references a member m_select_support that does not exist, so enabling that option should fail to compile (read from source, not built).
rank(i, c) assumes 0 <= i <= size() and does no bounds checking.

A search snippet claiming '2-3 times faster than the fastest known ones, for 1.5-5 times more space' belongs to the separate 'FM-index for Dummies' paper (Grabowski et al.), not to this project; do not quote it for wt_fbb.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick wt_fbb over QWT (C++ or Rust) or wavelet_forest only when you need a compressed, Huffman-shaped byte-alphabet FM-index inside an existing SDSL codebase and care about size; QWT has a published 2x win over SDSL on access/rank/select and supports select, so it is the safer choice for uncompressed, query-speed-first use.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing measurable was read this session: the repo has no numbers or benchmark code, the Algorithmica 2019 paper (and its arXiv 1104.3810 SPIRE 2011 precursor) could not be opened, and the only reachable text, search snippets of the abstract, says the new indexes are 'consistently fast and small relative to the state-of-the-art' with no ratio, compiler or hardware.
status_note: Abandoned research code (2 commits, last 2021-05-18, version 0.1.0) but MIT-licensed and a single ~1,900-line header, so it is easy to vendor into an SDSL project if you benchmark it yourself first.
sources_read: WebSearch: "Fixed Block Compression Boosting in FM-Indexes" pdf (snippets only)
